doc.title: Duffy Jackson interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, October 17, 1995

title: Rejoining under Thad Jones in 1985 and Frank Foster in 1989; jazz vaudevillians
summary: Return on crutches under Thad Jones, recovery in Florida with his father, and rejoining in 1989 with Frank Foster, ending after eighteen months.

story.theme_name: Playing with Count Basie: joining, leading, leaving
story.community_name: Playing with Count Basie: the band, its feel and its people

blocks.x: came back in January of 1985. Count had passed on and Thad Jones took over the band. And that was a very unique experience because the Count Basie Orchestra had never had another leader before. And there was a certain contingent in the orchestra that felt that they didn’t really need a leader. But in one way, to salvage all the work that was being canceled in many ways, the people didn’t want the Count Basie band without the Count. Although we still played the great music and unfortunately the band had to play for a lot less money, being that Count wasn’t there, and it was very difficult financially to keep the band out of bankruptcy. So they needed a great name like Thad Jones to come in and help the band and Thad was very interesting in the band in the first couple of months, because we didn’t really get together and rehearse right away. Thad just stood in front of the band and made announcements and counted off some tempos. Then all of a sudden he started to write some great arrangements, in my opinion not really in the style of the Basie band. But he was permitted to experiment and after a while it started to sound closer to what he was trying to do with Thad and Mel’s concept. And certain audiences said hey wait a minute, we want to hear the older Basie sound. But they were intrigued and you know, it was a very interesting time to be on the band. Now unfortunately I’d just had my surgery around eight or nine months before that or whatever — actually, I’m sorry, three months before I rejoined the Basie band — I got an emergency call that they needed me. And I was on crutches still, but you know what? If I was on my death bed I’d get up and play with the Basie band. I mean you know that was my dedication you know? So on crutches, I joined the band at the Blue Note in New York City, not knowing whether I’d get through the first number, the first set, the first night. And through the grace of God I built up my endurance and stamina to be able to play, and I lasted almost around I’d say around eight months before I needed to almost have my surgery re-done again. So I knew that physically it was not the time for me to try to make a comeback with the band. So I went down to Florida and played with my father. He was living in Vero Beach of all places. And for the next five months I played two nights a week with my dad, you know, three sets a day, you know, and then the other five nights I was bedridden, you know, just taking physical therapy to build myself back up. And then when it was time I went down to Miami and got into some gigs. And then when I really felt good enough, I went back to New York and said, “Hey, anybody remember me?” So I’ve had to come back from surgeries on a few occasions, but that’s what keeps me totally dedicated. Then coming back to the Basie band in 1989, with Frank Foster, I rejoined the band three days before we recorded the album “The Legend and Legacy of the Count Basie Orchestra,” which was nominated for a Grammy on Denon, a Japanese label. And it was a very big thrill to record an album with the Basie band with George Benson, “Big Boss Man” on Warner Brothers. And I played with the band for around © Fillius Jazz Archive -20-

eighteen months at that time, and then physically it started to break me down again, whatever, and I said well I think the time has come to let some younger drummers have an opportunity, you know. And I feel that if I can get in front of a group of musicians and not have to play the drums on every number, and play a little piano, a little bass, scat, work the crowd a little bit, like Dizzy used to do, you know, that’s sorely needed I feel in the industry. You know my father and I have been called the “jazz vaudevillians” in certain ways. Now in many ways, with the jazz purists, they felt that it was a little strange to be extroverted performers. But now you see all the great jazz players attempting to do a little shtick and get on the mic and talk a little bit to the folks. It’s sorely needed I feel, to bridge the gap right now.
Yeah. And I think if you’re familiar with the history of jazz that that’s where the music came from. It was music, but it was entertainment too.
You know, so I don’t think you have to apologize for putting some life into the music like that.
